PROSPECTS OF THE COTTON TRADE. Tux great strike in the Bolton cotton trade and he immense and artificial expulsion in the Oldham district are portentous symptoms of a state of things existing in one of our most important staple industries which may well compel reflection. The cotton trade is at the present time experiencing a crisis which it has not undergone for nearly forty years. The panics of 1847, 1867, and 1888, were nothing to the present condition of I affairs. These years of patio were times of monetary confusion when the bank rate of interest was as light as from eight to ten per cent., and when in fact discounting common bills of exchange was next to impossible. At the present time money is cheap. Good bills of exchange are negotiable at under three per cent, and yet we have cotton cheaper than it has been at any period for ' the last seventeen years, with the exception ef a short time last year. The question is a very serious one indeed, and Mr. Bright does I not overestimate the crisis The reduction of the hours of working by the late Factory Act, from sixty to fifty six and a half hours per week, is a very important matter. It amounts to about the _production of two ' millions of spindles. We are burning the candle at both ends at present, and Mr. Bright may well talk seriously upon the subject. During the last twenty five yearn the failures in the cotton trade have been something frightful. It is no exaggeration to *ay that one half of the cotton manufac- turers of Lancashire have failed to meet their engagements within the last twenty five years. There is little or no profit in the conduit of bounces at present. Neither im- porters of ootton, nor manufacturers, nor shipping merchants are making any profits.
